claim: Rice blast disease can cause the loss of enough rice to feed 212–742 million people annually.
source: This disease can cause the loss of enough rice to feed 212–742 million people annually (Fisher et al., 2012), and result in up to 100% yield loss in infected areas (Dean et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2012.

claim: Rice blast disease can result in up to 100% yield loss in infected areas.
source: This disease can cause the loss of enough rice to feed 212–742 million people annually (Fisher et al., 2012), and result in up to 100% yield loss in infected areas (Dean et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dean et al., 2012 and Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Rice is a staple food crop for greater than half the world's population.
source: The sustainability of rice production is critical, it is a staple food crop for greater than half the world's population.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about rice consumption globally.

claim: NLRs are a conserved component of plants' innate immune systems.
source: NLRs are a conserved component of plants' innate immune systems and survey the host environment for perturbations caused by invading pathogens (Dangl and Jones, 2001; Chisholm et al., 2006; Jones and Dangl, 2006; van der Hoorn and Kamoun, 2008; Dodds and Rathjen, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Most NLRs respond to the presence or activities of translocated pathogen effectors.
source: Most NLRs respond to the presence or activities of translocated pathogen effectors, proteins delivered by adapted pathogens to affect the physiology of the host to benefit the parasite (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010; Win et al., 2012; Wirthmueller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dodds and Rathjen, 2010; Win et al., 2012; Wirthmueller et al., 2013.

claim: The recognition event often results in a robust immune response and localised cell death.
source: The recognition event often results in a robust immune response and localised cell death, which limits disease caused by biotrophic pathogens on their hosts.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about NLR-mediated immune responses.

claim: Most NLRs comprise a multi-domain architecture with central nucleotide-binding (NB-ARC) and C-terminal LRR regions.
source: Most NLRs comprise a multi-domain architecture with central nucleotide-binding (NB-ARC) and C-terminal LRR regions.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about NLR structure.

claim: NLRs usually contain N-terminal coiled-coil (CC) or TOLL/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains.
source: They also usually contain N-terminal coiled-coil (CC) or TOLL/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains (Takken and Goverse, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takken and Goverse, 2012.

claim: In at least some cases, NLRs function in pairs to deliver disease resistance.
source: In at least some cases, NLRs function in pairs to deliver disease resistance, and these pairs can be tightly linked genetically (Eitas and Dangl, 2010; Cesari et al., 2014; Le Roux et al., 2015; Sarris et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eitas and Dangl, 2010; Cesari et al., 2014; Le Roux et al., 2015; Sarris et al., 2015.

claim: Most NLR pairs studied to date use one of the NLRs to detect the presence of specific effectors by direct binding.
source: Interestingly, most NLR pairs studied to date use one of the NLRs to detect the presence of specific effectors by direct binding (Kanzaki et al., 2012; Cesari et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kanzaki et al., 2012; Cesari et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2014.

claim: Integrated domains in NLRs show evolutionary relationships to putative virulence targets.
source: One mechanism by which this can be achieved is via unconventional integrated domains in the NLRs (known as integrated decoy or sensor domains) that show evolutionary relationships to putative virulence targets (Cesari et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cesari et al., 2014 and Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 100 NLRs in rice have been described to confer resistance to strains of M. oryzae.
source: To date, ∼100 NLRs in rice have been described to confer resistance to strains of M. oryzae, and 23 of these have been cloned (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: 23 rice NLRs that confer resistance to M. oryzae have been cloned.
source: To date, ∼100 NLRs in rice have been described to confer resistance to strains of M. oryzae, and 23 of these have been cloned (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Six M. oryzae effectors recognized by rice NLRs have been cloned to date: AVR-Pia, AVR-Pita, AVR-Pik, AVR-Pii, AVR-Piz-t and AVR1-CO39.
source: Identification of the pathogen effectors (also known as AVRs [avirulence proteins]) that are recognised by these NLRs has lagged behind and only six have been cloned to date, AVR-Pia (Yoshida et al., 2009), AVR-Pita (Orbach et al., 2000), AVR-Pik (Yoshida et al., 2009), AVR-Pii (Yoshida et al., 2009), AVR-Piz-t (Li et al., 2009) and AVR1-CO39 (Ribot et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the respective papers for each effector.

claim: AVR-Pia and AVR1-CO39 are recognised by the RGA4/RGA5 NLR pair.
source: AVR-Pia and AVR1-CO39 are recognised by the RGA4/RGA5 NLR pair (Okuyama et al., 2011; Cesari et al., 2013) through direct binding to a Heavy-Metal Associated domain (HMA, also known as RATX1) integrated into RGA5 after the LRR (Cesari et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Okuyama et al., 2011 and Cesari et al., 2013.

claim: AVR-Pia and AVR1-CO39 bind directly to a Heavy-Metal Associated domain (HMA) integrated into RGA5 after the LRR.
source: AVR-Pia and AVR1-CO39 are recognised by the RGA4/RGA5 NLR pair (Okuyama et al., 2011; Cesari et al., 2013) through direct binding to a Heavy-Metal Associated domain (HMA, also known as RATX1) integrated into RGA5 after the LRR (Cesari et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cesari et al., 2013.

claim: RGA4/RGA5 physically interact to prevent cell death mediated by RGA4 in the absence of AVR-Pia.
source: RGA4/RGA5 physically interact to prevent cell death mediated by RGA4 in the absence of AVR-Pia; the presence of the effector relieves this suppression (Cesari et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cesari et al., 2014.

claim: The presence of AVR-Pia relieves the suppression of RGA4-mediated cell death by RGA5.
source: RGA4/RGA5 physically interact to prevent cell death mediated by RGA4 in the absence of AVR-Pia; the presence of the effector relieves this suppression (Cesari et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cesari et al., 2014.

claim: The NLR pair Pik-1/Pik-2 recognises AVR-Pik.
source: Intriguingly, the NLR pair Pik-1/Pik-2, which recognises AVR-Pik (Figure 1) (Ashikawa et al., 2008; Yoshida et al., 2009), also binds the effector via an HMA domain but this domain is integrated between the CC and NB-ARC regions of Pik-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ashikawa et al., 2008 and Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: Pik-1/Pik-2 binds AVR-Pik via an HMA domain integrated between the CC and NB-ARC regions of Pik-1.
source: Intriguingly, the NLR pair Pik-1/Pik-2, which recognises AVR-Pik (Figure 1) (Ashikawa et al., 2008; Yoshida et al., 2009), also binds the effector via an HMA domain but this domain is integrated between the CC and NB-ARC regions of Pik-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and Figure 1B showing the domain architecture.

claim: The integrated HMA domains of RGA5 and Pik-1 appear to have evolved from a family of rice proteins that only contain the HMA domain.
source: The integrated HMA domains of RGA5 and Pik-1 appear to have evolved from a family of rice proteins that only contain the HMA domain (Cesari et al., 2013, 2014; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cesari et al., 2013, 2014 and Wu et al., 2015.

claim: The rice protein Pi21 contains an HMA domain that is not part of an NLR protein.
source: Interestingly, the rice protein Pi21, a disease susceptibility factor, contains an HMA domain that is not part of an NLR protein (Fukuoka et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fukuoka et al., 2009.

claim: Both AVR-Pik and the HMA region of Pik-1 exhibit nucleotide polymorphisms between pathogen isolates and rice cultivars that result in changes at the amino acid level.
source: Both AVR-Pik (Figure 1A) and the HMA region of Pik-1 exhibit nucleotide polymorphisms between pathogen isolates and rice cultivars that result in changes at the amino acid level (Yoshida et al., 2009; Kanzaki et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing polymorphisms.

claim: The interaction of AVR-Pik allele AVR-PikD with the Pik-1 NLR Pikp-1 is thought to be the oldest in co-evolutionary time.
source: The interaction of AVR-Pik allele AVR-PikD with the Pik-1 NLR Pikp-1 is thought to be the oldest in co-evolutionary time (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kanzaki et al., 2012.

claim: Cultivars of rice containing the Pikp allele are resistant to M. oryzae isolates expressing AVR-PikD.
source: Cultivars of rice containing the Pikp allele are resistant to M. oryzae isolates expressing AVR-PikD, but are susceptible to pathogen isolates expressing other AVR-Pik alleles (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kanzaki et al., 2012.

claim: Cultivars of rice containing the Pikp allele are susceptible to pathogen isolates expressing AVR-Pik alleles other than AVR-PikD.
source: Cultivars of rice containing the Pikp allele are resistant to M. oryzae isolates expressing AVR-PikD, but are susceptible to pathogen isolates expressing other AVR-Pik alleles (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kanzaki et al., 2012.

claim: The only structure known for a M. oryzae effector is that of AVR-Piz-t.
source: For example, the only structure known for a M. oryzae effector is that of AVR-Piz-t (Zhang et al., 2013), which adopts a six-stranded β-sandwich structure and contains a single disulphide bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: AVR-Piz-t adopts a six-stranded β-sandwich structure and contains a single disulphide bond.
source: For example, the only structure known for a M. oryzae effector is that of AVR-Piz-t (Zhang et al., 2013), which adopts a six-stranded β-sandwich structure and contains a single disulphide bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: There is no available structural information on domains from rice NLRs prior to this study.
source: To date, there is no available structural information on domains from rice NLRs, and no structural data from any system showing how plant pathogen effectors are directly recognised at the molecular level by an NLR.
evidence: This is presented as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: There is no structural data from any system showing how plant pathogen effectors are directly recognised at the molecular level by an NLR prior to this study.
source: To date, there is no available structural information on domains from rice NLRs, and no structural data from any system showing how plant pathogen effectors are directly recognised at the molecular level by an NLR.
evidence: This is presented as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The Pikp-HMA domain alone selectively interacts with the AVR-Pik allele AVR-PikD in yeast.
source: Here we show that the Pikp-HMA domain alone selectively interacts with the AVR-Pik allele AVR-PikD in yeast (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: Weak interaction was observed between Pikp-HMA and AVR-PikE in yeast.
source: Weak interaction was also observed with AVR-PikE (as evidenced by limited growth on the selective–LTH plate and some blue colouration in the X-gal assay), but not AVR-PikA or AVR-PikC, which is consistent with previous experiments (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: No interaction was observed between Pikp-HMA and AVR-PikA or AVR-PikC in yeast.
source: Weak interaction was also observed with AVR-PikE (as evidenced by limited growth on the selective–LTH plate and some blue colouration in the X-gal assay), but not AVR-PikA or AVR-PikC, which is consistent with previous experiments (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: AVR-PikD and Pikp-HMA form a stable complex in vitro that can be purified by analytical gel filtration.
source: Following expression, purification and verification of the proteins by intact mass spectrometry ('Materials and methods', Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Table 2), we showed that AVR-PikD and Pikp-HMA form a stable complex in vitro that can be purified by analytical gel filtration (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pikp-HMA can form a complex with AVR-PikE and AVR-PikA, but not AVR-PikC, as shown by analytical gel filtration.
source: Using this qualitative assay, we also found that Pikp-HMA can form a complex with AVR-PikE and AVR-PikA, but not AVR-PikC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pikp-HMA bound to immobilised AVR-PikD with a Kd of 31 ± 2 nM.
source: Using a multi-cycle kinetics approach, we found that Pikp-HMA bound to immobilised AVR-PikD with a Kd of 31 ± 2 nM (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: Pikp-HMA binds to AVR-PikE with an apparent Kd of 367 ± 41 nM.
source: For AVR-PikE, even though this was not fully saturatable under the conditions of our assay, we obtained an apparent Kd of 367 ± 41 nM, a greater than 10-fold weaker binding compared to AVR-PikD (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pikp-HMA binds to AVR-PikA with an apparent Kd of 710 ± 111 nM.
source: For AVR-PikA we could determine an apparent Kd of 710 ± 111 nM (also not saturatable in the assay).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data.

claim: Essentially no binding was detected for AVR-PikC to Pikp-HMA in the SPR assay.
source: We detected essentially no binding for AVR-PikC to Pikp-HMA in this assay (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The crystal structure of the Pikp-HMA/AVR-PikD complex was solved at 1.6 Å resolution.
source: Optimisation of one of these conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) produced crystals diffracting X-rays to 1.6 Å resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The Pikp-HMA/AVR-PikD complex reveals an intimate interface that buries 18.7% of the effector's solvent accessible surface area (1031.0 Å2).
source: The structure of the Pikp-HMA/AVR-PikD complex reveals an intimate interface formed between these proteins that buries 18.7% of the effector's solvent accessible surface area (1031.0 Å2, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 87.5% of AVR-PikD's buried surface area (902.2 Å2) is formed with a monomer of Pikp-HMA.
source: The majority of the interaction is formed with a monomer of Pikp-HMA, with 87.5% of the effector's buried surface area (902.2 Å2) and nine residues contributing hydrogen bond and/or salt bridge interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: Nine residues contribute hydrogen bond and/or salt bridge interactions between AVR-PikD and a Pikp-HMA monomer.
source: The majority of the interaction is formed with a monomer of Pikp-HMA, with 87.5% of the effector's buried surface area (902.2 Å2) and nine residues contributing hydrogen bond and/or salt bridge interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: No hydrogen bonds or salt bridge interactions are formed between AVR-PikD and the second monomer of the Pikp-HMA dimer.
source: No hydrogen bonds or salt bridge interactions are formed with the second monomer of the Pikp-HMA dimer.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: It is not possible for an AVR-PikD/Pikp-HMA heterotetramer (2:2 complex) to assemble due to steric clash.
source: Further, due to steric clash that would occur, it is not possible for an AVR-PikD/Pikp-HMA heterotetramer (2:2 complex) to assemble.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and inference from the crystal structure.

claim: Each Pikp-HMA monomer adopts the HMA-domain fold comprising a four-stranded antiparallel β-sheet and two α-helices packed in an α/β sandwich.
source: Each of the Pikp-HMA monomers adopts the HMA-domain fold (Pfam: PF00403), comprising a four-stranded antiparallel β-sheet and two α-helices packed in an α/β sandwich.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The closest structural homologue of Pikp-HMA is the HMA domain of yeast protein Ccc2A, overlaying with an r.m.s.d. of 1.58 Å over 72 residues.
source: The closest structural homologue of Pikp-HMA (defined by PDBeFold [Krissinel and Henrick, 2004]) is the HMA domain of yeast protein Ccc2A (Banci et al., 2001), overlaying with an r.m.s.d. of 1.58 Å over 72 residues (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HMA domains typically bind heavy metals or lighter cations such as Cu1+ or Zn2+ via two conserved Cys residues.
source: Typically, HMA domains bind heavy metals, or lighter cations such as Cu1+ or Zn2+, via two conserved Cys residues and are involved in metal transport or detoxification pathways (Bull and Cox, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bull and Cox, 1994.

claim: The conserved Cys residues for metal binding are not conserved in Pik-1 HMA domains, including Pikp-1.
source: Interestingly, these Cys residues are not conserved in Pik-1 HMA domains, including Pikp-1.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The Pikp-HMA structure does not contain a metal ion.
source: Hence, the Pikp-HMA structure does not contain a metal ion, and the loop between β1 and α1, which usually contains the metal-chelating Cys residues, is disordered.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The loop between β1 and α1 in Pikp-HMA is disordered.
source: Hence, the Pikp-HMA structure does not contain a metal ion, and the loop between β1 and α1, which usually contains the metal-chelating Cys residues, is disordered.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: AVR-PikD adopts a six-stranded β-sandwich structure, stabilised by a di-sulphide bond between Cys54 and Cys70.
source: AVR-PikD adopts a six-stranded β-sandwich structure, stabilised by a di-sulphide bond between Cys54 and Cys70.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: AVR-PikD contains an N-terminal extension comprising residues Arg31 to Pro52 prior to the start of the β-sandwich fold.
source: The effector contains an N-terminal extension, comprising residues Arg31 to Pro52, prior to the start of this fold (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A close structural homologue of AVR-PikD is AVR-Piz-t, with an r.m.s.d. of 2.33 Å over 58 aligned residues.
source: Database searches using PDBeFold reveals that a close structural homologue of AVR-PikD is AVR-Piz-t (Zhang et al., 2013), another M. oryzae effector protein, despite there being essentially no sequence identity between these proteins (r.m.s.d. = 2.33 Å over 58 aligned residues, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is essentially no sequence identity between AVR-PikD and AVR-Piz-t despite structural similarity.
source: Database searches using PDBeFold reveals that a close structural homologue of AVR-PikD is AVR-Piz-t (Zhang et al., 2013), another M. oryzae effector protein, despite there being essentially no sequence identity between these proteins (r.m.s.d. = 2.33 Å over 58 aligned residues, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Structural homology is observed between AVR-PikD and ToxB, a protein toxin from Pyrenophora tritici-repentis.
source: Further, structural homology is also observed to ToxB, a protein toxin from Pyrenophora tritici-repentis, the causative agent of tan spot in wheat (Nyarko et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison and a citation to Nyarko et al., 2014.

claim: The N-terminal extension of AVR-PikD appears to be unique.
source: In each case, the identified structural homology only extends to the β-sandwich fold and the N-terminal extension of AVR-PikD appears to be unique.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison and inference.

claim: AVR-PikDHis46 is bound in a pocket on Pikp-HMA via hydrogen bonds/salt bridge interactions with Pikp-HMASer218 and Pikp-HMAGlu230.
source: AVR-PikDHis46 is bound in a pocket on Pikp-HMA via hydrogen bonds/salt bridge interactions between AVR-PikDHis46:Nδ1/Pikp-HMASer218:Oγ and AVR-PikDHis46:Nε2/Pikp-HMAGlu230:Oε1; also, Pikp-HMAVal232 packs on top of the AVR-PikDHis46 ring and contributes hydrophobic/van der Waals interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pikp-HMAVal232 packs on top of the AVR-PikDHis46 ring and contributes hydrophobic/van der Waals interactions.
source: AVR-PikDHis46 is bound in a pocket on Pikp-HMA via hydrogen bonds/salt bridge interactions between AVR-PikDHis46:Nδ1/Pikp-HMASer218:Oγ and AVR-PikDHis46:Nε2/Pikp-HMAGlu230:Oε1; also, Pikp-HMAVal232 packs on top of the AVR-PikDHis46 ring and contributes hydrophobic/van der Waals interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg prevent the interaction with Pikp-HMA in yeast.
source: We found that AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg prevent the interaction (as observed on the -LTH selective growth plate and in the X-gal assay (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AVR-PikDIle49Glu maintains an interaction with Pikp-HMA in yeast.
source: However, AVR-PikDIle49Glu maintains an interaction and AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp showed intermediate binding (weak interaction on -LTH selective growth plate and in the X-gal assay [Figure 4A]).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp showed intermediate binding to Pikp-HMA in yeast.
source: However, AVR-PikDIle49Glu maintains an interaction and AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp showed intermediate binding (weak interaction on -LTH selective growth plate and in the X-gal assay [Figure 4A]).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No meaningful interaction was measured for AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg with Pikp-HMA by SPR.
source: Consistent with the Y2H results, we could not measure any meaningful interaction of AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg with Pikp-HMA (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AVR-PikDIle49Glu binds to Pikp-HMA with a Kd of 99 ± 18 nM.
source: For AVR-PikDIle49Glu and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp we were able to determine Kds of interaction of 99 ± 18 nM and 83 ± 16 nM respectively (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp binds to Pikp-HMA with a Kd of 83 ± 16 nM.
source: For AVR-PikDIle49Glu and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp we were able to determine Kds of interaction of 99 ± 18 nM and 83 ± 16 nM respectively (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The K60 (Pikp) rice cultivar is resistant to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikD.
source: As expected, the K60 (Pikp) cultivar is resistant to the M. oryzae Sasa2 line expressing AVR-PikD (Kanzaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Kanzaki et al., 2012.

claim: The K60 (Pikp) cultivar showed an intermediate phenotype to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikE.
source: We observed that the K60 (Pikp) cultivar showed an intermediate phenotype between susceptible and resistant to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikE.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The K60 (Pikp) cultivar was susceptible to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg.
source: For the mutants, we found that the K60 (Pikp) cultivar was susceptible to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg, but resistant to those expressing AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The K60 (Pikp) cultivar was resistant to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp.
source: For the mutants, we found that the K60 (Pikp) cultivar was susceptible to M. oryzae Sasa2 lines expressing AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala and AVR-PikDAsp66Arg, but resistant to those expressing AVR-PikDAla67Asp and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Co-expression of Pikp-1, Pikp-2 and AVR-PikD is required to observe robust features of cell death in N. benthamiana.
source: In this system we required the co-expression of Pikp-1, Pikp-2 and AVR-PikD to observe robust features of cell death, including necrotic tissue and accumulation of phenolic compounds that give rise to auto-fluorescence (Figure 6B) (Bos et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of individual proteins or any combination of protein pairs (Pikp-1, Pikp-2, AVR-PikD) did not result in significant cell death in N. benthamiana.
source: We did not observe significant effects in N. benthamiana leaves following expression of the individual proteins or any combination of protein pairs (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Co-expression of AVR-PikE, AVR-PikA and AVR-PikC with Pikp-1 and Pikp-2 fails to elicit a cell death response in N. benthamiana.
source: Further, co-expression of AVR-PikE, AVR-PikA and AVR-PikC with Pikp-1 and Pikp-2 fails to elicit a cell death response (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala, AVR-PikDAsp66Arg and AVR-PikDAla67Asp mutations do not elicit a cell death response when co-expressed with Pikp-1 and Pikp-2 in N. benthamiana.
source: Using this approach, we found that the AVR-PikDHis46Glu, AVR-PikDArg64Ala, AVR-PikDAsp66Arg and AVR-PikDAla67Asp mutations do not elicit a response, but AVR-PikDIle49Glu and AVR-PikDPro47Ala/Gly48Asp still promote cell death (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.
